title: Gather the scattered
hookLine: sound the great shofar for freedom and gather the scattered

lines: A LINE THAT SPEAKS TO THE MAP.
cards: Pull up a map of where Jewish families have lived. Babylon and Baghdad. Cordoba and Toledo.
Fez, Cairo, Aleppo, Sana'a. Vilna, Kraków, Odessa. Cochin on the coast of India.
Then Brooklyn, Buenos Aires, Johannesburg, Melbourne. One Shabbat table can hold a recipe from Aleppo and a lullaby from Vilna. Some families carry two or three of those names in their own story.
In all of those places, every weekday, the same line of the Amidah has spoken directly to that map.

teach.b: The tenth blessing says: sound the great shofar for our freedom.

teach.h: RAISE A BANNER FOR THE EXILES.
teach.b: Raise a banner to gather our exiles, and gather us together from the four corners of the earth. Blessed are You, who gathers the dispersed of Your people Israel. The great shofar comes from the prophet Isaiah.
In the old Jewish translation: "it shall come to pass in that day, that a great horn shall be blown," and the lost and the scattered come home to worship in Jerusalem.
The banner is Isaiah's too: a signal raised high, so people far away can see where to come. Notice the first word of the blessing isn't gather. It's teka: blow.
The shofar is the sound of the Jubilee year, when slaves went free and land returned to its families.
So freedom comes first, then gathering.

teach.h: FROM MY TROUBLES TO OUR STORY.
teach.b: Here the requests turn toward the whole people's future, from my troubles to our story.
The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, says it follows the blessing of the years because a prophet promised that when the land bears fruit again, the exiles will be near.
Jews have said these words in Baghdad and Vilna and Cochin, far from Jerusalem.
In modern times, some see the return of Jews to the land of Israel in this light, and others read the blessing as pointing to a future not yet here.
Either way, every weekday, scattered people ask to be gathered.

how: Teka beshofar, the request to gather the exiles, is the tenth blessing of the weekday Amidah, said three times a day; communities differ in how they relate it to the modern State of Israel.

o: blow: the shofar's call that opens the tenth blessing
the Jubilee year when land returns to families
a ram's horn kept in the Temple for festivals

games.q: inside the tenth blessing — tap the pairs.
p: a signal for the far away

s: the blessing's first word is gather
it's teka, blow: freedom comes first, then gathering.
the great shofar is an image from Isaiah

games.q: you're writing a request for a scattered people to come home. what comes first in the Amidah's version?
o: a request for wealth for the journey.
games.why: teka beshofar gadol: sound the great shofar for our freedom. the Jubilee horn, which set slaves free, opens the way.

practice: Call up the face of someone you love who lives far away: a sibling across the country, a grandparent in another land, a friend who moved and slowly went quiet.
Picture where they are right now, what time it is there, and imagine for a moment the whole table together again. If you pray, you can hold them in this blessing.
